title: Homer’s Iliad & Odyssey, Part I
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: Colton Cauthen opens a series of essays on the primary sources in his three-year Great Books reading plan with Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, read for the first time in his late thirties. He offers a mix of plot summary and honest reflection rather than a scholarly interpretation. His central observation is that honor, which Plato, Boethius and Aquinas recognised as a deep human desire, springs from two sources in the Iliad: a just intuition that honor should go to the honorable, and a corrupting pride that quickly demands honor for itself. He traces how that pride drives Agamemnon and Achilles toward rage, destruction and the sacrifice of the many for the few, and how the Odyssey further undercuts the romance of everlasting glory when Achilles tells Odysseus he would rather be a living farmhand than a king of the dead. He ends by noting that he now wants to reread the Iliad, which he takes as a case for rereading great books.
points: Cauthen reads the great works directly, as primary sources, rather than reading about them, and values coming to them with little background.
In the Iliad honor has two sources, justice and pride, and the second corrupts the first, producing Achilles' ruinous rage.
The epic accepts the sacrifice of the many for the few, from the slaughter of Achaeans to exalt Achilles to the gods who watch men suffer untouched.
The Odyssey challenges the glory ideal when Achilles in the underworld says he would rather be a poor living farmhand than rule over the dead.
His wish to reread the Iliad after first judging he never would is offered as an argument for rereading the great books.
quotes: Instead of reading about the greatest thinkers of the past, I wanted to hear from them directly, so I compiled a list of primary sources and got started.
The end result of striving for honor seems to be death and destruction.
It would seem that honor is a good, but that its pursuit and attainment are plagued with an excessive, dangerous pride which can lead to further grief and suffering.
In the opening book of the Iliad, Homer seems to draw out the two sources for man’s desire for honor: justice and pride.
If this is the rightly ordered desire for honor, then the second motivation, pride, is the corruption of that otherwise good desire.
In the Iliad, both the gods and the story’s hero accept, without hesitation or reservation, the idea of sacrificing the many for the few.

When I finished reading the Iliad, I felt sure it was not one I would ever reread. I enjoyed it, and had some appreciation for its value, but I couldn’t see myself returning to it for another full read.
